Unpopular opinion: the better analogy for me here may be Appel and Haken’s 1976 proof of the four color theorem.

Part of that proof relied on computer checks that humans couldn’t realistically verify by hand. At that time, many mathematicians were uncomfortable with it, not necessarily because they thought the result was false, but because it shifted what counts as a proof.

In hindsight, computer-assisted proof didn’t ruin mathematics. It pushed the community to refine standards around verification, reproducibility, and trust in tools.

So I don’t think "AI proof" is the real issue. The issue, in my opinion, is the communication around it. This was clearly managed and shaped by OpenAI scientists, and OpenAI shouldn’t understate that human role in the public narrative.

The bottleneck will be global class field theory. The work of Golod and Shafarevich needs the existence of the Hilbert class field (a consequence of global class field theory, although historically earlier and perhaps easier) and also the Poitou-Tate long exact sequence and global Tate duality (harder than class field theory, or perhaps equal to class field theory depending on what your definition of class field theory is). Note that Poitou-Tate and global Tate duality are also both essentially needed in all known proofs of FLT, but are pre-80s. Lean currently doesn't have enough machinery to even state these results, but we're close. The proofs are however another matter. I have been flagging global class field theory as an important goal for years now but we've been working on the (much easier) local case for a year now and are still not done.

Clarification: basically we need the material in the first 20 slides of these notes from one of the lectures in my FLT course from earlier this month https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT/blob/main/2026_EPSRC_TCC_course/20260507.pdf . Group cohomology we have, and the topology on an infinite Galois group we have. Continuous cohomology we're close to having but we don't have. With all those in place we will be able to state the 9-term exact sequence on slide 19. The hard part is proving this, which will be a huge endeavour; it is done e.g. somewhere in Neukirch--Wingberg--Schmidt "cohomology of number fields" (it is too advanced for Cassels--Froehlich).

(For less prominent results, a messy autoformalised proof might at least provide evidence to humans that a claimed AI proof is correct and so might be worth starting the digestion process on. A short note from inside big tech (FAIR, Meta), adding a perspective rather than relitigating points made well above.

A small nuance on the formalization side: for many people, the primary reason to formalize a result is to check that it is correct, but doing so is expensive enough that people who actually invest in formalization today may do so because they value the digestion it forces. Those motivations aren't the same thing, and AI may shift the balance: if generation gets cheap and verification stays expensive, the case for formalization-as-correctness gets stronger even when nobody is in it for the digestion.

What I'd add from this side: I'm genuinely glad to see resources flowing into pure mathematics, even when the incentives between industry labs and the community only partially overlap. They don't need to fully overlap for everyone to be working toward the same goal: satisfying the kind of curiosity that draws people into mathematics in the first place. Our group at FAIR would genuinely like to find common ground with the community on this, with the caveat that everyone has limited bandwidth and has to pick where to engage. I agree with @Daniel Sautot that the substantive issue is the communication around AI-assisted work rather than its existence, and the transparency concerns raised by @Joseph Myers and @Jack McCarthy are real, I wish industry could be as transparent as possible on cost, on what didn't work, on what the systems do badly.

Two of the most interesting cases of human formalization to check correctness of a non-AI proof were also cases that ended up with substantial digestion / changes to the informal proof: for both the Kepler conjecture and consistency of NF (where the normal mathematical community processes had failed to yield a clear conclusion on the correctness of the proof), the informal proof corresponding to the final formalization was quite different from the original informal proof. It might be interesting to see what autoformalization does in those cases when asked to formalize the original proofs: whether it manages to push through the difficulties and produce a formalization closer to the original version, whether it runs into trouble, or whether the existence of the second-generation formalized proofs in the training data contaminates things too much and the AI can't resist following the revised proofs instead whenever it has difficulties.

There are different ways to interpret the word "digestion." The examples by Joseph Myers illustrate improved mathematical understanding that came as a kind of "side effect" of formalization. While obviously valuable to the mathematical community, I suspect that if some superhuman entity (I leave it to the reader to choose "AI" or "God" or "the devil") had offered the bargain, "I'll give you the formal proof for free, and it will convince all skeptics, but you won't learn anything mathematical from it," then Hales and Holmes might very well have accepted. So I still think these are primarily examples of formalization-as-correctness, with "digestion" being a happy byproduct, but one that both parties might willingly forgo "for the right price."

Building Mathlib, however, is a different kind of "digestion." The aforementioned superhuman bargain would surely be rejected by people who are trying to build a high-quality Mathlib. It's here where I think the difference between motivations is most worrisome. "Big tech" certainly understands the value of carefully developed libraries, but seems to be having trouble fighting off the threat of AI slop, even for software libraries that "big tech" cares about a lot more than Lean's Mathlib.

I didn't mean for "you won't learn anything mathematical" to be taken literally. I just meant that we're currently facing a realistic possibility that formalization projects that would previously have yielded new mathematical insights and cleaner proofs as a matter of course, might now be completed at low cost (at least by some measures of cost) while yielding far less insight / reusable code.

Maybe the distinction is not just correctness vs. digestion, but whether the attempt compounds.

A one-off autoformalized proof may certify a result but leave little behind. A good formalization attempt should leave reusable memory: definitions, prerequisite maps, failed routes, named obstructions, small verified lemmas, and a clear account of the residual gap. Even if the theorem is not yet formalizable, that residual map can make the next attempt cheaper.

So the question might be: what artifact should an AI-assisted formalization leave behind when the full proof is currently out of reach?

Hi all. Question about gradient stability in training. Instead of gradient clipping or normalization, has anyone tried a structural approach — replacing the division by zero (that causes NaN) with an indexed form that preserves the algebraic structure?

I've been working on something called RICIS where F/0 → ∞_F (typed infinity). The gradient division becomes 0_F/0_G → F/G after structural cancellation. It's O(1) and formally verified in Lean 4.
